conceptTag: Will customers stay if prices rise 10%?
readerTitle: Raise prices 10%: who stays, who walks?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (재사용 운반 상자 제조·물류 회사와 그 회사의 추적 앱 구독) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 가격 인상의 결과는 '고객'이 아니라 고객별 대안, 지출 비중, 시간에 따라 갈린다. 그래서 고객을 나눠서, 충분히 오래 지켜보며 판단한다.
misconception: 고객에게 물어보면 몇 명이 떠날지 알 수 있고, 인상 후 한 달 동안 아무도 안 떠나면 더 올려도 된다.

sources.text: 미시경제학의 표준 개념 (가격 탄력성의 결정 요인: 대체재, 지출 비중, 시간)
모든 수치와 회사는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 상자 계산 확인: 기존 가격 $20 − 변동비 $12 = 공헌이익 $8. 인상 후 $22 − $12 = $10. 같은 이익을 내는 판매량 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8, 즉 판매량이 20% 줄어도 이익 동일. 매출은 100개 × $20 = $2,000에서 80개 × $22 = $1,760으로 줄어듦.
앱 구독: $200 → $220 (+10%). 60일 사전 공지와 갱신 시점 적용은 설명용 설정입니다.
'단기보다 장기에 수요가 더 탄력적이다'는 일반 원리로 서술했으며 특정 연구 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Raise prices 10%: who stays, who walks?
body: You run a company that makes reusable plastic crates and rents them to food producers. You deliver them, collect them and wash them. You also sell a small app that tracks where every crate is.
Plastic, fuel and wages are all up. You need prices about 10% higher. Over the next few cards, you make the calls.

image.label: Stacks of crates on a truck, with a phone showing a tracking map
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 색깔 있는 플라스틱 운반 상자가 트럭 짐칸에 쌓여 있고, 옆에 상자 위치가 점으로 표시된 지도 화면의 휴대폰. 상자 위에 "+10%" 태그가 살짝 붙어 있음. 실제 기업 로고 없음.

cards.title: How do you predict who will stay?
body: Before any letter goes out, you want a sense of how customers will react. Your sales lead has three ideas.

options.text: Email a survey: "Would you still buy if prices rose 10%?"
options.feedback: Quick and cheap. But people answer surveys differently from how they act, and some will say "no" just to push back on the price.

options.text: Sort customers by how easily they could switch: their other options, what share of their costs crates are, and how hard it is to change
options.feedback: This looks at the forces that actually drive reactions. It takes an afternoon with your account list, and it shows you where the risk sits.

options.text: Raise prices for everyone and see what happens
options.feedback: You learn the truth fast, but you learn it by losing customers you might have kept.

cards.title: First, how many crates can you afford to lose?
body: Same profit at 80 crates as at 100. So you could lose up to **20% of volume** and still earn the same, even though revenue drops from $2,000 to $1,760.
How sensitive buyers are to price is called **price elasticity**. Your job now is to find out who is sensitive.

breakdown.label: Old price per crate rental
breakdown.detail: $8 left after $12 of costs that come with each rental

cards.callout: Lose more than that and the raise costs you money. Lose less and it pays.

cards.title: Your list splits into two groups.
body: **A grocery chain** rents 40% of your crates. Crates are a visible cost line for them, and two rivals have already sent them quotes.
**Small farms** rent the rest. Crates are a tiny part of their costs, and no one else near them offers pickup and washing. What do you do?

image.label: One big buyer on a seesaw against many small farms
image.brief: 시소 일러스트. 한쪽에는 큰 마트 건물 하나(경쟁사 견적서 두 장을 들고 있음), 다른 쪽에는 작은 농장 여러 개. 마트 쪽에 "Many options", 농장 쪽에 "Few options" 라벨. 실제 로고 없음.

options.text: Raise 10% for everyone. Same rule, no arguments
options.feedback: Simple and easy to explain. But the chain is the customer most able to leave, and losing 40% of volume is twice what your math allows.

options.text: Raise farms 10%. Offer the chain 5% in exchange for a two-year volume commitment
options.feedback: You get the full raise where buyers have few options and lock in the account that could walk. The cost: the chain learns it can bargain, so be ready for that next time.

options.text: Raise farms 15% and freeze the chain's price
options.feedback: Farms have fewer options, not none. A bigger jump invites them to shop around, and a freeze tells the chain you back down easily.

cards.title: The app looks easy. Raise it again?
body: Say you chose B. You also raised the tracking app from $200 to $220 a month per site, with 60 days' notice.
One month later, cancellations are normal. Your team says users clearly don't care. They want another 10%.

options.text: Yes. No one left, so demand isn't price sensitive
options.feedback: Most users haven't hit renewal yet, or looked for alternatives. Stacking a second raise now could trigger the exits the first one was quietly building.

options.text: Wait through a full renewal cycle. Track cancellations, downgrades and sites removed
options.feedback: Reactions grow over time as customers find and test other options. Waiting costs a few months of extra revenue but shows you the real answer.

options.text: Roll the raise back to be safe
options.feedback: You give up money you're probably able to earn, and you signal that your prices aren't firm.

cards.title: Your sorting is a guess, not a measurement.
body: Who can switch changes. A rival might open a washing depot near your farms next year. A cheap tracking tool could appear. The chain's quotes could get better.
Sorting customers by risk only tells you where to look. Keep checking real behavior: who renews, who orders less, who starts asking for quotes.
And charging groups differently only works if you can explain why. A farm that hears the chain got 5% will want a reason.

cards.title: Six months later.
body: The chain signed for two years. A few farms complained, and almost all stayed. App renewals came in slightly lower than before, well within what the higher price covered.
The raise worked not because customers "accepted" it, but because you priced each group by how easily it could leave.

image.label: A simple chart line rising gently with a few dips
image.brief: 부드러운 선 그래프. 6개월 동안 이익 선이 완만하게 오르고, 중간에 작은 하락 두 번. 아래에 "Chain: signed", "Farms: stayed", "App: small dip at renewal" 메모 스티커.

cards.title: Price sensitivity lives in each customer's options.
body: Each decision used one idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1:** elasticity depends on substitutes, share of spending and switching effort, not on what people say
**Decision 2:** different groups have different willingness to pay, so one price change lands differently
**Decision 3:** demand gets more sensitive over time, so judge a raise over a full cycle
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list your ten biggest customers. Next to each, write how many real alternatives they have. Start any price review there.
